current: "Thoria is the highest-melting oxide known and glows brightly in lantern mantles."
corrected: "Thoria is the highest-melting oxide known; mixed with 1% ceria it glows brightly in lantern mantles."
reason: Pure thoria emits poorly in the visible. The bright mantle glow comes from the small cerium oxide addition, so the current sentence is misleading.
source: Welsbach mantle chemistry (99% ThO2 + 1% CeO2); Ivey 1974 and standard texts

reason: CID 9905479 is cerium(III) oxide (Ce2O3), not cerium(IV) oxide CeO2.
source: PubChem PUG REST: CID 9905479 = Ce2O3 'Cerium oxide'; CID 73963 = CeO2 'Ceria'

current: SrTiO3 becomes a superconductor below about 0.3 K.
corrected: "Lightly electron-doped SrTiO3 becomes a superconductor below about 0.3 K."
reason: Pure, stoichiometric SrTiO3 is an insulator. It superconducts (Tc about 0.1–0.4 K) only when electron-doped, for example by oxygen vacancies or Nb or La substitution.
source: Schooley et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 12, 474 (1964); Collignon et al., Annu. Rev. Condens. Matter Phys. 10, 25 (2019)

current: Bronze Age traders shipped tin ore across Europe from Cornwall.
corrected: "Bronze Age traders carried Cornish tin across Europe, often as smelted ingots."
reason: The evidence for long-distance tin trade is mostly smelted tin ingots, not raw ore, and a Cornish origin for much of it is still debated. Saying ore was shipped overstates the evidence.
source: Archaeometallurgical studies of Bronze Age tin ingots (e.g. Salcombe, Uluburun; Berger et al., PLoS ONE 2019)

current: Magnesium sulfate is one of the main salts in seawater after sodium chloride.
corrected: "Magnesium sulfate is one of the main salts in seawater, after sodium chloride and magnesium chloride."
reason: As written, the sentence implies MgSO4 is the second most abundant salt. Magnesium chloride actually comes second and MgSO4 third, so the ranking is misleading.
source: Standard sea-salt composition (e.g. CRC Handbook / oceanography texts): NaCl ~78%, MgCl2 ~11%, MgSO4 ~5%, CaSO4 ~4% by mass

reason: Terminal Cr–O bond order in dichromate averages 5/3 (about 1.67), not 1.5. The same correction applies to the other five terminal bonds, bonds[3] through bonds[7], each [x, y, 1.5] -> [x, y, 1.67]. The coordinates themselves check out: Cr–O(bridge) is 1.79 Å, Cr–O(terminal) is 1.63 Å, Cr–O–Cr is 126° and the angles are tetrahedral.
source: Formal bond-order count for Cr2O7 2- (Cr(VI): 1 bridging single bond + 5 bonding pairs shared over 3 terminal O = 5/3); file convention elsewhere uses exact averages (NO3- 1.33, CO3 2- 1.33, MnO4- 1.75)

corrected: "RaCO3 + 2 HCl -> RaCl2 + CO2 + H2O (Curie turned radium-bearing sulfates into carbonates, dissolved them in HCl, then purified the chloride by fractional crystallization)"
reason: The current value has no actual reaction (an ellipsis) and cannot be checked for balance. The convention requires a real, balanced equation.

current: Promethium gives three electrons, like all lanthanides.
corrected: "Promethium gives three electrons, like most lanthanides."
reason: Not every lanthanide behaves this way: Eu and Yb commonly form +2 ions and Ce forms +4, so 'all' is misleading.
source: Greenwood & Earnshaw, Chemistry of the Elements (lanthanide oxidation states)

current: Promethium chloride is a rare glowing salt of the only radioactive lanthanide.
corrected: "Promethium chloride is a rare glowing salt of the only lanthanide with no stable isotopes."
reason: Other lanthanides also have radioactive isotopes, including naturally occurring ones such as Sm-147 and Lu-176. What sets Pm apart is that it has no stable isotope.

current: Dry blue CoCl2 turns pink as it absorbs water and becomes [Co(H2O)6]2+.
corrected: "Dry blue CoCl2 turns pink as it absorbs water, forming the hydrate CoCl2·6H2O."
reason: The pink solid hexahydrate contains trans-[CoCl2(H2O)4] units plus two lattice waters, not [Co(H2O)6]2+. The hexaaqua ion forms only in solution.

current: Some bacteria and birds use magnetite crystals to sense Earth's magnetic field.
corrected: "Some bacteria use magnetite crystals to sense Earth's magnetic field, and some animals may too."
reason: Magnetotactic bacteria are well established. Magnetite-based magnetoreception in birds is unproven: the iron-rich cells found in pigeon beaks turned out to be macrophages.

current: 99Mo -> 99mTc (molybdenum-99 decays in a generator; eluted with saline as NaTcO4)
corrected: "99MoO4 2- -> 99mTcO4- + e- (beta decay of molybdate in a generator; eluted with saline as NaTcO4)"
reason: As written, the equation is not balanced: it leaves out the beta electron and the charge change. Writing it as molybdate decaying to pertechnetate balances both the mass number and the charge.
Anhydrous CoCl2 has a PubChem record (CID 3032536), so the field should not be null.

current: The most abundant mineral family in Earth's crust: quartz, sand, flint, opal.
corrected: "One of the most common minerals in Earth's crust: quartz, sand, flint, opal."
reason: Feldspars, not the silica minerals, are the most abundant mineral family in the crust. Quartz comes second.
source: USGS / standard mineralogy texts (feldspars make up roughly half the crust; quartz is about 12%)

corrected: "Almost all synthetic; it also occurs as the very rare natural mineral qusongite."
reason: WC does occur in nature as the mineral qusongite. Calling it simply 'Synthetic' is incomplete and clashes with its 'Minerals & ores' category.
